title: Human-in-the-loop patterns and idempotency
summary: Put a person in the loop where an action is costly or irreversible, and make every side effect safe to retry with idempotency keys or compensating steps. Exactly-once is a design goal built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers.
useIf: An agent can spend money, change data, message people or call tools whose effects cannot be undone, and runs can be retried or resumed.
avoidIf: Do not gate every harmless read behind approval. Approval fatigue turns the gate into a rubber stamp.

explain.md: OWASP's Excessive Agency entry names three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy. One concrete weakness is an extension that fails to independently verify and approve high-impact actions, such as a deletion that needs no confirmation from the user [[tr10]]. A human approval gate is the standard control. In Agent Framework, a function wrapped in `ApprovalRequiredAIFunction` makes the agent run complete with a response that says what input is needed, and the caller returns the decision in a new run [[tr13]]. Workflows use a `RequestPort` and `RequestInfoEvent` in C#, or `ctx.request_info()` in Python, and route the response back to the requesting executor [[tr12]]. LangGraph uses `interrupt()` [[r44]], and Magentic offers plan sign-off [[r10]].

explain.title: Approval gate and idempotent execution
explain.alt: The agent proposes an action. The gate asks a human to approve the exact arguments. After approval the tool runs once with an idempotency key, and a retry returns the saved result.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Agent
  participant G as Gate
  participant H as Human
  participant T as Tool
  A->>G: Propose action and args
  G->>H: Ask approval for exact args
  H-->>G: Approve
  G->>T: Execute with idempotency key
  T-->>A: Result
  A->>T: Retry, same key
  T-->>A: Saved result, no second effect

explain.md: Idempotency makes retries safe. Stripe's design: the client generates the key (up to 255 characters), a retry with the same key returns the saved response, and v1 keys can be pruned after at least 24 hours [[r26]]. The Compensating Transaction pattern covers what retries cannot: when a later step of an eventually consistent operation fails, undo the completed steps [[r27]]. Use both for agent tool calls with side effects. The key must be stable across retries, for example derived from run id and step id, not a fresh random value per attempt.

explain.title: Bind approval to the exact arguments
explain.md: If the agent can change the arguments after the human approved, the approval covers nothing. Show the final arguments, approve a hash of them, set an expiry, and reject execution if they differ.

whereToUse: Payments, refunds, deletions, deployments and outbound messages
Long-running workflows that wait hours or days for a reviewer
Tools that call third-party APIs that support idempotency keys
Multi-step operations that need compensation if a later step fails
Regulated flows that need a record of who approved what

use: Actions are costly, irreversible or externally visible
Runs can retry, resume or replay
A reviewer can judge the action from what the gate shows
avoid: Approving every read-only call, which causes fatigue
Using approval as a substitute for least-privilege tool permissions
Random idempotency keys that change on every retry
flips: Approval volume overwhelms reviewers: tier by risk and batch low-risk approvals
Actions are reversible and high volume: sample audits and compensations instead of gates
Reviewers lack context: show intent, arguments, evidence and consequences

pitfalls.cause: Too many low-risk prompts cause approval fatigue
pitfalls.fix: Gate only above a risk threshold, show a clear summary and measure the rejection rate.

pitfalls.symptom: A retry creates a second charge or message
pitfalls.cause: No idempotency key, or a new key was generated for each attempt [[r26]]
pitfalls.fix: Derive the key from run and step ids, and have the tool or its API store results by key.

pitfalls.symptom: A partly finished operation leaves inconsistent state
pitfalls.cause: A later step failed and nothing undid earlier steps [[r27]]
pitfalls.fix: Define a compensating action per step and run them in reverse order on failure.

pitfalls.symptom: The approved action differs from the executed one
pitfalls.cause: Arguments changed between approval and execution
pitfalls.fix: Approve a hash of the final arguments, set an expiry and verify before execution.

scenarios.title: Irreversible payment action
scenarios.situation: An agent can issue refunds through a payment API. A refund cannot be recalled, runs can be retried after crashes, and finance wants to know who approved each one.
unknowns: Does the payment API support idempotency keys?
How long may an approval wait?
scenarios.question: What do you implement?

options.name: Approval on the exact arguments plus a stable idempotency key per run and step, stored with the approver identity
options.why: The gate stops unwanted refunds, the key stops duplicates on retry and the record meets the audit need.
options.tradeoff: Latency while waiting for a person, and key handling per API.

options.name: Autonomous refunds with logging only
options.why: Logs cannot undo a refund, and a retry could pay twice.
options.tradeoff: Right for small reversible credits under a hard cap.

options.name: Approval only, no idempotency key
options.tradeoff: A crash after approval can lead to a duplicate on resume.

flips.if: Refunds under a small threshold are routine
flips.then: Auto-approve under the threshold, gate above it and audit samples.

flips.if: The API has no idempotency support
flips.then: Keep your own ledger of executed step ids and check it before calling.

scenarios.takeaway: Gate the decision, and make the execution safe to repeat.

scenarios.title: High volume, mostly harmless
scenarios.situation: A workflow agent performs thousands of actions per day: most are reversible tagging and labelling, a few delete records. Reviewers already complain about approval prompts.
unknowns: What is the cost of a wrong delete?
scenarios.question: How do you place the human?

options.name: Risk-tiered gates: approve deletes, auto-approve reversible actions with logging and sample audits, and make deletes soft where possible
options.why: It focuses human attention where damage is real and keeps throughput for the rest.
options.tradeoff: Tiering rules need tuning, and sample audits detect rather than prevent.

options.name: Approve every action
options.why: Fatigue turns approvals into rubber stamps while throughput collapses.
options.tradeoff: Right while the agent is new and volume is low.

options.name: No approvals, rely on compensating undo
options.tradeoff: Hard deletes cannot be undone, so they still need a gate or a soft-delete design.

flips.if: Deletes can be soft with a retention window
flips.then: Compensate by restoring and reduce gating.
Raise the threshold and sample more.

scenarios.takeaway: Spend human attention on irreversibility, not volume.

quiz.q: A tool wrapper creates a new random idempotency key for every attempt of the same logical charge. What is the result?
options: A retry after a timeout can create a second charge
quiz.explain: Idempotency works only when retries reuse the same key, so the service returns the saved response. A fresh key each attempt makes every retry look like a new request. Derive the key from run and step ids. [[r26]]

quiz.q: Which statement about exactly-once execution is the most accurate?
options: A checkpoint on its own guarantees exactly-once
You can get the effect through at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers, or compensations
Exactly-once is automatic in all durable runtimes
quiz.explain: Resuming or retrying can repeat a step, so safety comes from idempotency keys and compensations on top of checkpoints. Approval gates control whether an action runs, not how many times. [[r26]][[r27]]

quiz.q: Which are root causes of Excessive Agency in OWASP's description?
quiz.explain: OWASP lists excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy as the typical root causes. Logging is not among them. Approval gates address autonomy and high-impact actions. [[tr10]]
